page.itineraries:
Day 1 — Arrival in Seoul: Cheonggyecheon Stream and Myeongdong Orientation
Arrive in Seoul throughout the day and check into your hotel. There are no planned activities until the evening, allowing time to settle in and navigate the city at your own pace. At 6 pm, gather for a welcome meeting with your CEO and fellow travellers. This is your opportunity to meet the group, ask questions about the tour ahead, and get oriented to the basics of moving around Seoul.

Following the meeting, join your CEO for an orientation walk through the city centre. You'll start at Cheonggyecheon Stream, an 8.4-kilometre waterway and public space that runs through downtown Seoul. The walk passes nearly two dozen overhead bridges and small waterfalls—a quieter counterpoint to the urban density surrounding it. Your CEO will point out practical essentials: where to find supermarkets, main squares, and ATMs. These details matter when navigating a city on foot and by public transport.

From Cheonggyecheon, the walk continues into Myeongdong, a neighbourhood that operates at full intensity regardless of the hour. The streets form a dense grid packed with street food carts, major shopping malls, and entertainment venues. This is where you'll encounter Seoul's retail and food culture firsthand—vendors selling traditional snacks to contemporary fashion occupy nearly every corner.

Note that this tour requires comfort with spending most of the day on your feet and carrying your own luggage through busy train stations and streets. South Korea's train system forms the backbone of inter-city travel on this itinerary, so familiarity with moving efficiently through public spaces is essential.

After the orientation walk, you have the option to join fellow travellers for a group dinner to end your first evening. Otherwise, Myeongdong itself offers numerous dining choices if you prefer to wander independently. Check the hotel lobby notice or ask reception for the exact meeting time and location before heading out.

Day 2 — Seoul's Royal Heritage: Palaces, Traditional Villages, and Historic Quarters
Begin your Seoul exploration with a guided bus tour across the city's most significant districts, where centuries of Korean history remain visible amid the modern metropolis. Gyeongbokgung Palace, constructed in 1395 as the principal royal residence of the Joseon Dynasty, anchors this journey. Despite repeated destruction over the centuries, more than half of the palace's structures remain standing or have been meticulously restored. Within its expansive grounds sit two essential museums: the National Palace Museum and the National Folk Museum, which together chronicle the traditions and history of the Korean people during the Joseon era.

From the palace, venture into Bukchon Hanok Village, a neighbourhood that reflects approximately 600 years of Seoul's history. This area contains the city's largest concentration of privately owned traditional Korean wooden homes, known as hanok. Walking through its interconnected narrow alleys reveals the architectural care invested in these structures—small courtyards, decorative outer walls, and distinctive dark tiled roofs appear around nearly every corner, with roughly half a dozen alleyways showcasing particularly careful restoration work.

Next, visit Insadong Alley, one of Seoul's most established quarters. The narrow passages that wind through this historic area once housed the royal studio for painters during the Joseon Dynasty. Today, the alley operates as a cultural destination filled with antique shops, contemporary galleries, traditional tea houses, and restaurants serving authentic Korean cuisine. The blend of old and new here reflects Seoul's character.

The afternoon offers flexibility for independent exploration and optional activities suited to your interests. Gwangjang Market, one of South Korea's oldest and largest traditional markets, houses more than 5,000 shops and is particularly renowned for its fabric selection and authentic Korean street food—an ideal destination for those seeking to experience local market culture and taste specialties like bibimbap, soondae, and kimchi. Alternatively, the Seoul Museum of History provides a comprehensive overview of the city's evolution from the Stone Age to the present day, featuring interactive exhibits including a large floor map of Seoul useful for planning further exploration.

Breakfast is included. You will stay at Hotel Prince or a similar property.

Day 3 — High-Speed Train to Gyeongju: Temple Arrival and Overnight Stay
Board a high-speed train after breakfast for a two-hour journey south through the countryside to Gyeongju, the former capital of the Silla Kingdom for 1,000 years. The ride offers views of rural South Korea at a moderate pace before arriving at this historic city.

Upon arrival, settle into Golgulsa Temple for an overnight stay in a traditional ondol room. These spaces are heated for comfort, with beds made directly on the floor. Rooms are arranged in single-gender dormitories, shared among group members.

Your first evening introduces you to temple life. A traditional dinner prepared in the temple kitchen precedes a session on temple etiquette—the customs and practices that structure daily life here. You'll also observe a martial arts performance by resident monks, gaining insight into the physical discipline that complements spiritual practice.

In the morning, participate in the daily drum and bell ritual that marks the start of the monastic day. If you wish, take an easy hike up to Korea's only stone cave temple for guided meditation as the day breaks. Breakfast follows, completing your introduction to temple routines.

This overnight stay offers direct encounter with monastic practice—not as observer, but as temporary participant in the rhythms that have sustained this community for centuries.

Day 4 — Gyeongju: Temple, Observatory, and Royal Tombs
Begin with a peaceful morning meditation and martial arts practice, followed by a traditional drum and bell ritual before venturing into Gyeongju. Travel by private vehicle to visit the city's most significant historical landmarks.

Bulguksa Temple, a UNESCO site set on the slopes of Mount Toham, serves as a head temple of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism. The complex encompasses seven National treasures of South Korea, among them the Dabotap and Seokgatap stone pagodas, the Cheongun-gyo bridge, and two gilt-bronze statues of Buddha. Each element reflects the architectural and artistic standards of the Silla period.

In the heart of Gyeongju, the former capital of the Silla Kingdom, Cheomseongdae Observatory rises as a modest but significant structure. Dating to the seventh century, it remains one of East Asia's oldest surviving astronomical observatories. This stone tower was used to observe celestial patterns and forecast weather, serving as a cornerstone of the region's ancient scientific practice.

The Daereungwon Tomb Complex concludes your exploration. Within its rolling mounds and gardens lie 23 burial sites, the most notable being Cheonmachong and Hwangnamdaechong. These tombs contain thousands of relics exceeding 1,500 years in age, offering insight into royal Silla Dynasty life and the artistic standards of the period. The artifacts within document the customs, craftsmanship, and hierarchy of this ancient civilization.

Settled at Swiss Rosen Hotel Gyeongju (or similar) for the evening.

Day 5 — Yangdong Folk Village, Haedong Yonggungsa Temple and Busan Arrival
Depart Gyeongju-si by private vehicle for the 90-minute journey to Busan, a coastal city that combines modern development with historical significance. En route, visit Yangdong Folk Village, a UNESCO site within Gyeongju National Park. Founded in the early 1400s, this 500-year-old village preserves more than 160 homes showcasing traditional Joseon Dynasty architecture. Walking through its lanes offers a window into early Joseon life, with well-maintained structures set against a natural backdrop that has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

Continue toward the coast to reach Haedong Yonggungsa Temple, a Buddhist temple built directly into cliffsides overlooking the East China Sea. Originally constructed in 1376, this 14th-century structure ranks among Korea's frequently photographed temples, its seaside location creating an atmosphere of contemplation. Local tradition suggests that prayers offered here grant at least one wish. The temple complex invites quiet exploration of its halls and courtyards, and a traditional market nearby offers local snacks for those seeking an authentic taste of the region.

Upon arrival in Busan, settle into your accommodation at Felix Hotel by STX (or similar). An orientation walk introduces you to Haeundae Beach, one of Busan's most visited coastal areas, and nearby Dongbaek Island, home to the APEC House—a modern architectural structure offering views across the shoreline.

The evening is yours to experience Busan's culture. Opt to unwind at a jjimjilbang, a traditional Korean spa bathhouse featuring an array of hot spring tubs designed to rejuvenate body and mind. Alternatively, embrace the Korean tradition of noraebang—karaoke rooms where you can sing in private with friends. For those seeking additional activities, consider a night yacht ride cruising along Busan's illuminated coastline, or visit Busan Tower Observatory, where 360-degree views from its 120-metre height reveal the city's scale and geography. The tower, standing 69 metres above sea level, features a design inspired by the baldaquin of Dabotap Pagoda in Bulguksa Temple, linking this modern landmark to Korea's architectural heritage.

Day 6 — Busan's Markets and Culture Village; Return to Seoul
This day bridges two cities, beginning in Busan before the afternoon train journey to Seoul. The morning unfolds across several distinct neighbourhoods, each revealing different layers of the port city's character and commerce.

Start at Jagalchi Fish Market, the major market anchored at Nampo Port. This is where Busan's seafaring heritage becomes visible—rows of stalls display fish, octopus, and shellfish. The market operates with particular activity as locals and fishmongers negotiate prices. The sensory environment is deliberate and direct: the salt air, the calls of vendors, the volume of marine life on display.

From there, move to Gukjesijang, commonly known as Gukje Market, which sits near BIFF Square, Busan's well-known film district. This market carries historical weight. It emerged during the Korean War as a place where refugees could earn a living, and that origin remains part of its identity. Today it functions as a bustling international market where food stalls, home goods, clothing, and souvenirs create a dense, layered shopping environment. The market's evolution from necessity to thriving commerce reflects Busan's own trajectory.

Next is Yongdusan Park, a green space with deliberate design. The park's unique silhouette is said to resemble a dragon's head, and it contains over 70 different types of trees. The 118-metre Busan Tower rises from within the park, visible from across the city. This combination of natural landscape and architectural landmark creates a distinct sense of place in the urban fabric.

Gamcheon Culture Village offers a different visual environment. Set into the side of a mountain, the village is defined by its pastel-coloured houses, hand-painted murals, intimate cafes, and small shops. The village was born from necessity—residents originally settled here without formal planning—but has developed into a cultural area while maintaining its residential character. Walking through its narrow streets reveals both the artistic interventions and the lived reality of the neighbourhood.

By late morning, board the high-speed train for the 2.5-hour journey to Seoul. This efficient transit allows the day to encompass two cities without excess travel time consuming the itinerary.

Upon arrival in Seoul, visit Namdaemun Market, Korea's oldest traditional market. Dating to 1414, it has operated for over six centuries, and that longevity shows in its scale: over 10,000 vendors operate across several city blocks, making it the oldest and largest traditional market in the country. The density of commerce and the variety of goods—food, textiles, everyday items—reflect the market's role as a genuine centre of city life, not merely a tourist destination.

The remainder of the day offers several options. The cable car ascends to N Seoul Tower, Seoul's most recognised landmark, positioned at the top of Mt Namsan at 480 metres above sea level. Originally a broadcasting station, it now functions as a public observatory. The structure itself—standing 236.7 metres tall atop the 243-metre mountain—has appeared frequently in Korean television dramas and films. An additional fee grants access to the observation deck, where a 360-degree panoramic view encompasses the entire city.

Alternatively, spend time in Gangnam District, a neighbourhood that combines historical significance with ongoing development. Gangnam Station, one of Seoul's busiest subway hubs, contains an extensive underground shopping centre. The district also offers Bongeunsa, a Buddhist temple situated in the neighbourhood's centre, providing a counterpoint to the commercial activity. Restaurants throughout the district reflect both local and international cuisines.

Two other options complete the evening: Banpo Bridge, home to the Moonlight Rainbow Fountain Show—the world's longest bridge fountain, featuring nearly 10,000 LED lights and 380 water-spraying nozzles that synchronize with music and create different configurations throughout the day. By night, the fountain transforms into a display of coloured water jets. Alternatively, visit the Floating Islands, a culture complex comprising three man-made islands near Banpo Bridge, surrounded by LED lighting that creates a distinctive night-time visual effect.

Breakfast is included. Accommodation is at Hotel Prince or similar.

Day 7 — The Korean Demilitarized Zone and War Memorial
Begin with a private vehicle transfer to the Demilitarized Zone, the de facto border between North and South Korea established in 1953. Spend about 3-4 hours visiting the Demilitarized Zone, the de facto border between North and South Korea. Created as a Cold War boundary, the DMZ's lack of civilian development has allowed natural habitat to recover, creating an unexpected wildlife refuge within one of the world's most geopolitically significant borders.

Return to Seoul for the second portion of the day. Visit the War Memorial of Korea, a substantial complex divided into indoor and outdoor exhibits. The memorial preserves approximately 9,000 artifacts documenting Korea's military history and the Korean War, offering historical context for those interested in the nation's past.

The remainder of your afternoon and evening are yours. Rest at your accommodation or venture independently through Seoul. Those seeking additional activities can visit the Samsung Leeum Contemporary Gallery, navigate the diverse Itaewon neighbourhood, or participate in a pre-booked kimchi-making and Hanbok (traditional Korean dress) experience.

Overnight in Seoul at Hotel Prince or similar. Breakfast included.

Day 8 — Seoul to Jeonju: Hanok Village and Traditional Korean Dinner
Begin with a free morning in Seoul before heading to the train station for your high-speed journey to Jeonju. The bullet train carries you across the country, delivering you to one of Korea's best-preserved traditional towns.

Upon arrival in Jeonju, enter the hanok village—a quarter of wooden-frame houses with distinctive curved tile roofs that reflect centuries of Korean residential architecture. Your guided tour takes you through the town's principal landmarks: Gyeonggijeon Shrine, an important historical site; Jeondong Catholic Church, a structure blending Eastern and Western architectural traditions; the Korean Liquor Museum, where you'll learn the history of traditional Korean beverages; and the Jeonju Handicraft Exhibition Hall, showcasing the region's artisanal production.

As evening descends, settle in for a Hanjeongsik traditional dinner—a full-course Korean meal that unfolds across multiple small banchan (side) plates. Each dish reflects Korean culinary tradition, allowing you to taste the depth and diversity of the cuisine in one sitting.

You'll spend the night in a traditional hanok accommodation within the village, allowing the experience to fully settle.

Optional activities are available if you wish to deepen your cultural engagement. Consider donning a Hanbok—the traditional Korean dress—and photographing yourself in the village streets in full regalia, with traditionally styled hair. Alternatively, visit the Hanok Village Craft Museum to engage in hands-on traditional crafts: create hanji (Korean handmade paper), shape your own ceramic piece on a pottery wheel, practise calligraphy with brush and ink, or craft and paint a traditional fan with designs inspired by flowers, birds, and landscapes.

Meals included: Breakfast and Dinner

Day 9 — Damyang Bamboo Forest and Boseong Green Tea Fields to Yeosu
Today marks a shift from urban environments to South Korea's countryside. Travelling from Jeonju in a private vehicle, you'll head toward the coast with stops at two of the region's defining landscapes.

page.subtitle: Village trekking, temple exploration, and tea estates from Sigiriya to Yala National Park
page.summary: This 11-day itinerary moves through Sri Lanka's interior and southern regions, staying in community-based lodges and family-run guesthouses rather than resort chains. The route connects Sigiriya's archaeological zone with Kandy's temple district, then ascends into the central highlands via train to the tea-growing regions of Bandarawela and Haputale, before descending to the wildlife sanctuary at Yala and the coastal village of Bentota. Days center on walking—village trekking, tea estate trails, mountain passes, and monastery approaches—alongside stays in local homes and conservation-focused lodges. The pace is deliberate, with transfers by road, rail, and foot, and with participation in local activities: lake fishing, cookery in a private residence, early-morning game drives, and overnight treks through mist-covered terrain.

Guided trek to Embekke, Gadaladeniya, and Lankathilake temples in the surrounding hills. Overnight at Thotupola Residence.

Day 5 — Kandy to Bandarawela: Train Through the Highlands
Transfer to Peradeniya Railway Station for a train departure at 12:30 PM southbound into the central highlands. The 3-hour journey ascends through tea plantations and mountain passes to Bandarawela. Meet the driver at Bandarawela station for transfer to The Hideaway, a guesthouse in the town center.

Day 6 — Tea Estates & Ella Rock Trail
Morning trek through Haputale's working tea estates, afternoon ridge walk up Ella Rock with views of the southern highlands. Overnight at The Hideaway in Bandarawela.

Day 7 — Haputale to Horton Plains: Two-Day Trek Commencement
Transfer from Bandarawela to Haputale trailhead. Begin two-day trek toward Horton Plains National Park and Ohiya, ascending through high-elevation terrain with overnight in a rural homestay. Trek includes moderate difficulty.

Day 8 — Horton Plains Trek Conclusion & Transfer to Yala
Completion of second-day trekking through Horton Plains National Park to Ohiya station. Transfer southward to Yala (approximately 3 hours). Overnight at Hibiscus Garden Hotel in Tissamaharama, the gateway town to Yala National Park.

Day 9 — Yala National Park Game Drive & Bentota Transfer
Early-morning game drive in Yala National Park with picnic breakfast. Transfer to Bentota (approximately 5 hours). Overnight at Amal's homestay.

Day 10 — Weligalpoththa Buddhist Monastery Trek
Walking trek from Bentota to Weligalpoththa Buddhist Monastery, a temple site located in inland terrain. Overnight in a village house near the monastery.

Day 11 — Return to Bentota
Departure from the village house and return transfer to Bentota, marking the end of the tour.

source.summary: Discover Xi'an's historic highlights over this 3-day all inclusive tour with your private guide. Board an included bullet train to Xi'an, explore the fascinationg Muslim Quarter. Visit the Great Mosque, walk around the Ancient City Wall, tour the Terracotta Warriors and admire Big Wild Goose Pagoda.
source.itineraries:
Day 1 Beijing/Xi'an - Bullet train to Xi'an, Great Mosque, Muslim Quarter
Your guide in Beijing will greet you in your hotel lobby at 07:30 am, and then you'll head to the train station for a 6-hour journey to Xi'an. Arriving in Xi'an check into the hotel. Then today’s adventure starts with a visit to the Great Mosque which is the most significant mosque in China and is a fascinating blend of Chinese and Islamic architecture and aspects. It was constructed during the Hongwu reigion of the Ming dynasty, with further additions during the Qing dynasty. Previous religious complexes are known to have stood on the same site, dating back as far as the Tang dynasty.
Later, take a walk around the Muslim quarter, home to the Hui Muslim community for centuries. Stroll through these narrow streets dotted with small shops, halal butchers, sesame-oil factories, small mosques markets and restaurants.

Accommodation:
• Manxin Hotel Bell Tower or similar (2 nights)
Meals Included:
• Lunch
Day 2 Xi'an - Terracotta Warriors & Big Wild Goose Pagoda
Morning set off to visit the Terracotta Warriors. You will learn about this incredible archaeological find, discovered in 1976 by farmers digging a well, after being buried for 2,000 years. Three main pits are open for you to view, where just under 2,000 of the total 6,000 warriors – each individually sculpted from clay, each having a different costume, height, and even facial expression – stand in battle formation.
After marveling at this incredible display we will enjoy lunch in a local village before our private transport takes us to the Big Wild Goose Pagoda. Once, the pagoda held old Buddhist relics and classics brought from India by the hierarch Xuanzang. If you are lucky you may catch a fantastic musical fountain show at the north square of the temple.

Accommodation:
• Manxin Hotel Bell Tower or similar (2 nights)
Meals Included:
• Breakfast, Lunch
Day 3 Xi'an/Beijing - Ancient City Wall, bullet train back to Beijing
Spend the morning exploring the ancient City Wall. This is the most significant and best-preserved city wall extant in China, running over 13 kilometers around Xi'an. Opt to bike around the wall which takes around 2 hours.
Then it's a 6-hour journey back to Beijing by bullet train. In late afternoon, you will arrive Beijing West Railway Station where the trip ends.

Meals Included:

page.itineraries:
Day 1 — Beijing to Xi'an: Great Mosque and Muslim Quarter
Your guide meets you in your Beijing hotel lobby before dawn to reach the train station for a six-hour journey south on the high-speed rail to Xi'an. On arrival, you settle into your accommodation, then begin with the Great Mosque, the most significant mosque in China. The structure dates to the Hongwu period of the Ming dynasty, with subsequent additions during the Qing; earlier religious complexes occupied this same ground as far back as the Tang dynasty, creating a palimpsest of architectural intent. The building fuses Chinese and Islamic elements throughout. Afterward, a walk through the Muslim Quarter introduces the narrow streets where the Hui Muslim community has lived for centuries. Sesame-oil factories, halal butchers, small neighbourhood mosques, market stalls, and restaurants line the passageways, creating a self-contained commercial and cultural enclave distinct from the surrounding city.

Day 2 — Terracotta Warriors and Big Wild Goose Pagoda
The morning is devoted to the Terracotta Warriors, the clay army discovered in 1976 when local farmers dug a well and broke through a buried vault. Of the estimated 6,000 warriors created for the emperor's afterlife, just under 2,000 stand visible across three main excavated pits. Each figure was hand-sculpted from clay with individual costume, height, and facial expression — a staggering exercise in repetition and variation carried out over two millennia ago. After examining the site, lunch takes place in a local village restaurant. Your private transport then carries you to the Big Wild Goose Pagoda, a seven-story structure that once held Buddhist relics and classical texts brought westward from India by the Tang monk Xuanzang. If timing allows, the musical fountain performance at the temple's north square provides a contemporary counterpoint to the ancient site.

Day 3 — Ancient City Wall and Return to Beijing
The final morning visits Xi'an's Ancient City Wall on foot or by bicycle. The wall extends 13 kilometers in circumference and ranks as China's most significant and best-preserved example of its type, running the perimeter of the historic centre. A bicycle circuit takes roughly two hours. By afternoon, you depart Xi'an on a six-hour northbound high-speed rail journey, arriving at Beijing West Railway Station in late afternoon where the tour concludes.
